sn55.23:1.2: There is a Sakyan lady named Kāḷīgodhā (“black iguana”), whose son is Bhaddhiya ([ud2.10](), [an1.193]()). She features in [sn55.39]() and [thag16.7](), where she is repeatedly referred to as _godhā_. In the current Sutta, the individual is referred to as _godhā sakko_, with the name in feminine but the clan in masculine. The same readings are found in BJT. Now, while Pali allows nominatives in apposition to be of different genders, it prefers agreement, as seen in _kāḷigodhā sākiyānī_ of [sn55.39:1.3](), where the masculine form of the clan has been adapted to the feminine name. I think the inverse has happened here: the name has been adapted to masculine in agreement with the clan, but this is in flux. This is seen in the Sinhalese manuscripts cited in footnotes in the PTS edition, which use the masculine vocative _godha_ and insert the masculine honorific _bho_, with some variations and inconsistencies. I think the insertion of _bho_ is a tell that that manuscript tradition edited the text to be masculine. I think there was only one Godhā, a woman. Since here she is named following Mahānāma, the form of her name was mistakenly adapted to his, creating a tension in the text, which editors have addressed inconsistently. See too [sn47.19:1.4](), where the text’s female was made male in the commentary.
sn55.23:3.2: Mahānāma is, of course, correct, but curiously the Buddha’s reply is not recorded.
